title: The Name on the hard road
hookLine: the Name helps on the long road where all else fails (Sukhmani 2)

lines: A TOSAA: FOOD WRAPPED IN CLOTH.
WHAT DO YOU TAKE ON THE HARDEST ROAD?
cards: A long journey on foot: days of dusty road between towns, no signpost you can trust, no inn guaranteed. Before setting out, a traveler needs a tosaa, a bundle of provisions wrapped in cloth.
Nobody sensible leaves without one. Sukhmani's second ashtpadi knows that world.
It takes the traveler's bundle, the dark road, the burning sun, the stranger's town, and asks what you'd want with you on the hardest road of all.

teach.h: DISTANCE: THE NAME IS YOUR FOOD.
teach.b: The stanza is a string of journeys, each with its own danger, and each answered by the Name. In paraphrase: on the road whose miles cannot be counted, the Name of God is your provisions.

teach.h: DARKNESS: THE NAME IS YOUR LIGHT.
teach.b: On the road of utter darkness, the Name of God is the light with you. On the road where no one knows you, the Name of God is there to recognize you.

Where the heat is fierce and the sun burns, the Name of God is your shade. Where thirst torments you, the Name of God rains down like nectar. Five dangers: distance, darkness, being a stranger, heat, thirst.
Every one gets an answer. The word for provisions is tosaa, the bundle from the hook.
So the Name is food when the road is too long, light in the dark, a familiar face in a town of strangers, shade at noon, water when you're parched.
Some readers hear this as the journey after death, the road the previous stanza began. Others hear it in life too. A long illness has miles that can't be counted.
Depression can be a road of utter darkness.

teach.h: A STRANGE TOWN: THE NAME KNOWS YOU.
teach.b: Moving to a new country is a town where no one knows your name.

teach.h: HEAT AND THIRST: SHADE AND RAIN.
teach.b: The stanza doesn't say the road will be shortened, or that you can skip it.
It promises company on it, and provisions for it.

how: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this stanza within the second ashtpadi, and some return to it during long illnesses, journeys and other hard stretches of life.

o: a lamp carried to light a long dark path
a traveler's provisions, a bundle for the road
a resting place for travelers by the road

games.q: the dangers of the road — tap the pairs.

s: the stanza promises the hard road will be shortened
it promises provisions and company on the road, not a shortcut.
tosaa means provisions for a journey
the bundle of food a traveler carried; the stanza says the Name is that.
some readers hear the road as the soul's journey after death
others hear it in the hard roads of life too.

games.q: you're on a road so long its miles can't be counted, and your bundle of food is gone. what does the stanza say is with you?
o: the Name of God as your provisions.
games.why: on the road whose miles cannot be counted, the Name of God is your provisions, your tosaa, there.

practice: Think of one hard thing ahead, a long shift, a difficult call, a stretch of caring for someone, and pick the image from the stanza that fits it: food for the long road, light in the dark, a known face, shade, rain.
Say that image to yourself slowly three times, adding Waheguru if you pray, and breathe with it, as if packing it like a bundle in cloth.

wordCard.voice: Tosaa, a traveler's provisions: in Sukhmani's second ashtpadi, the Name is food on the endless road, light in the dark, a friend among strangers, shade in the heat, rain in the thirst.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: tosaa, a traveler's provisions; the stanza says the Name is your tosaa on the endless road.

carryVoice: Your line: company on the road. The road stays long, and the bundle is packed. Day four hundred forty-four.
